old: The study looks at whether the separation can be maintained with a structured report for review, using a modular Graph RAG prototype. It contributes a retrieval workflow that mixes graph and textbook candidates, explicit handling of missing patient facts, and a verifier that checks pinned source records. We report successful component checks along with remaining diagnostic limitations. The work concerns a general claim review architecture. Its narrow source collection limits what has been tested.
draft: This study examines evidence provenance and uncertainty handling in a clinical review prototype. Its implemented contributions are traceable source-identity checks, preservation of missing or conflicting patient facts, and bounded medication-warning rules. We separate these checks from general passage entailment and patient applicability. Development experiments compare functioning retrieval configurations and medication-decision paths; earlier broken configurations document recovery after defect repair. The goal is to measure useful supported decisions alongside incorrect support and abstention, without claiming clinical validation or diagnostic superiority.
humanized: This study examines evidence provenance and uncertainty handling in a clinical review prototype. It implements traceable source-identity checks, preserves missing or conflicting patient facts, and applies bounded medication-warning rules. These checks are kept separate from passage entailment and patient applicability. Development experiments compare functioning retrieval configurations and medication-decision paths; historical runs document recovery after defect repair. The evaluation measures useful supported decisions, incorrect support and abstention. No claim of clinical validation or diagnostic superiority is made.

old: Just identifying a source is not enough when it comes to clinical claim review. A checksum may pick up on changed bytes, but it can't verify that a passage supports a recommendation or is relevant to a specific patient. The TRIPOD-LLM guideline was used to guide our reporting of the model settings, the evaluation data and the limitations [7]. ALCE assesses the generated answers together with the quality of the citations, making a distinction between citation support and the mere presence of references [8]. SciFact separately evaluates whether scientific evidence supports or contradicts a claim and identifies the reasons for that [9]. These tasks make clear the limits of our implementation: it only checks the identity of the pinned source and a limited number of medication rules, while arbitrary clinical claims are not verified. We have not carried out an independent evaluation of general semantic support nor completed the validation needed for clinical use.
draft: Source identity, semantic support and patient applicability require separate evaluation. ALCE assesses citation quality [8], and SciFact tests scientific claim support [9]. MedRAGChecker combines textual natural language inference with biomedical graph compatibility for claim-level verification [17]. CRITIC-RAG incorporates a verifier into medical retrieval and generation [18], while MedRAG/MIRAGE examines medical retrieval configurations [19]. Our implementation checks pinned source identity and a small medication-rule set; it does not implement general clinical entailment verification. The contribution must therefore be assessed through bounded warning decisions and uncertainty handling, rather than through citation integrity alone.

old: The active textbook collection consists of 1,134 passages from the local First Aid and Pathoma text files, taken from the MedQA textbook release [5]. Text was divided into 150-word chunks with a 20-word overlap. S-PubMedBert-MS-MARCO generates 768-dimensional embeddings for cosine search in Qdrant [12]. Dense retrieval retrieves 20 candidates, which are reranked by a local cross encoder to keep five passages [13]. Ingestion records source hashes and chunk identifiers. The presence of the dataset does not grant the right to redistribute the underlying books. The repository does not contain the text of the books. Acquisition and reuse terms require separate checking.

The revised text and graph plus text results therefore rose by 22.2 and 25.0 percentage points respectively. These development gains followed combined changes to ingestion, linking, ranking, prompting and output handling. It is not possible to determine which of the changes led to the improvement. Output processing was successful in all 108 revised synthesis responses as compared with five failures prior to revision. However, even after successful processing one text RAG case and two graph plus text cases remained without a ranked diagnosis.

old: As Table 3 shows, global reranking improved the early retrieval results for the development probes, with precision at rank one increasing from 0.600 to 0.900 and micro recall among the top five results rising from 0.667 to 1.000. For all four drug label queries, the reranking method retrieved a directly relevant passage at rank one, whereas in the previous ordering the first relevant passage for each of them was at rank six. The MRR at ten also increased from 0.667 to 0.925.

old: All 12 of the query-passage pairs that were directly relevant appeared in the first five results; at a cutoff point of ten, however, only 12 out of 100 of the retrieved pairs were directly relevant, which meant that the full context precision was 0.120. The developer fact checklist stayed completely covered with 13 out of 13 facts included. These results relate to the availability of passages and facts in a small, known corpus, and they do not prove that the generator has carried out faithful interpretation or that retrieval quality extends across the entire textbook collection. The measures of precision, recall, hit rate and MRR rely on direct answer relevance, while nDCG also takes into account related passages by means of graded gains.

old: We created a prototype of a retrieval augmented clinical review system which keeps a record of the sources used and maintains a state of uncertainty whenever patient information is missing. Candidate information is provided by means of graph and textbook retrieval, and separate verification checks are carried out using pinned source records and bounded medication rules. During the development phase we used 36 examination vignettes, ten retrieval queries, 108 synthetic medication cases and 158 provenance controls and alterations. When compared to the answer key, the LLM on its own achieved an agreement of 18 out of 36, text retrieval gave 19 out of 36 and graph plus text retrieval yielded 17 out of 36; exploratory paired tests did not provide evidence of a difference between the approaches. The revised implementation recovered all 72 of the expected warning events and retained uncertainty in all 24 of the cases where the allergy information was unknown or conflicting within the original set of synthetic cases. All 26 of the valid provenance controls were accepted and all 132 of the constructed alterations were rejected. Because these datasets were used to guide debugging, the figures reported here are development and regression results and not the results of independent validation. The repairs restored candidate retrieval and corrected observed extraction failures, without demonstrating a diagnostic benefit from the graph. Further clinical review and testing on cases that had not been touched are still necessary; general clinical claim support and patient applicability have not been validated.
draft: We evaluated a clinical review prototype that separates source identity, missing patient information and bounded medication-warning rules. A development comparison reused 108 synthetic cases with the same fixed proposal and label passages. Exact warning-and-support decisions matched developer labels in 108/108 cases for deterministic extraction plus rules, 81/108 for LLM-only, 106/108 for production LLM extraction plus rules, and 83/108 for rule-filtered LLM warnings. Failed attempts remained in all-case denominators. Filtering improved warning precision but reduced recall to 63.9%, illustrating the need to report useful decisions alongside incorrect support. In the separate 36-vignette diagnosis study, LLM-only, text retrieval and graph plus text obtained 18/36, 19/36 and 17/36 matches; no diagnostic advantage was established. Source-identity controls accepted 26/26 valid inputs and rejected 132/132 alterations. The results document implementation behavior and recovery after defect repair on reused development material. They do not establish general semantic verification, clinical prescribing safety or independent generalization. The hybrid did not improve exact-case performance over the deterministic baseline.

For production LLM extraction plus rules it matched 106 out of 108. For rule-filtered LLM warnings it matched 83 out of 108. Failed attempts remained in the all-case denominators. Filtering made the warning precision better. The recall dropped to 63.9 %. This illustrates the need to report useful decisions alongside incorrect support. Source-identity controls accepted all 26 valid inputs and rejected all 132 altered inputs. These results show how the system behaves and recovers after fixing a bug on the development data. They do not prove semantic checking, clinical prescribing safety or independent generalization. The hybrid method did not make exact-case performance better than the deterministic baseline.

old: The four repaired cases had the note "No allergy history was recorded." Keeping the allergy status unknown fixed a failure that was seen in the unchanged regression suite. For the 108 cases a lexical baseline had warning precision of 43 out of 85 (50.6 %) and recall of 43 out of 72 (59.7 %). Deterministic extraction and intended-facts checks each had precision and recall of 72 out of 72. The lexical comparator ignores negation and medication timing; its lower score does not prove an LLM benefit. The tests gave all label passages and a fixed proposal. They did not use LLM extraction, live retrieval, treatment generation or independent prescribing-safety validation.

old: This prototype separates candidate retrieval from source integrity checks and keeps missing allergy information inside a limited medication-rule scope. Development checks recorded repaired retrieval, output processing and extraction behavior. Development checks did not show that the graph improves agreement with the answer key or that real citations give clinical support. The next evaluation must test useful supported decisions, as well as wrong support and abstention on cases that were written by others and reviewed by clinicians. Until those results come the system should be called a development prototype.
draft: The prototype provides traceable source-identity checks and bounded medication-warning decisions while preserving uncertainty. On reused development cases, production extraction plus rules produced more exact decisions than LLM-only warnings, but did not improve on deterministic extraction plus rules. Post-generation filtering reduced incorrect support at the cost of useful coverage. Historical diagnosis changes represent recovery after defect repair, without an established graph advantage. These findings motivate independent case authorship and clinical review before generalization claims; they do not validate arbitrary clinical entailment or prescribing safety.
